title: April 6 Deadline Forces Hormuz Open
description: Trump's April 6 energy-strike deadline proves to be the decisive pressure point. As the deadline approaches, the administration communicates through Swiss and Omani channels that failure to permit shipping transits will result in direct strikes on Iranian oil and gas infrastructure — the one category of targets excluded so far. Iran's remaining leadership calculates that losing oil infrastructure (their only post-war revenue source for reconstruction) is worse than the humiliation of permitting transits. A tacit agreement emerges: Iran stops mining operations and permits limited convoy transits through cleared channels under US naval escort. Tanker traffic resumes at ~30% of pre-war volume by late April, rising to ~60% by June. Oil prices retreat from $113 to $95-100 within weeks of reopening, settling at $90-95 by summer as SPR releases and alternative routing cover the remaining gap. The worst economic scenarios are averted, though global growth still takes a hit.

title: Prolonged Hormuz Blockade
description: Iran holds firm. Despite catastrophic military losses, the regime calculates that Hormuz closure is its only remaining strategic leverage — the one card that gives the US and its Gulf allies a reason to negotiate rather than simply destroy Iran completely. Mine-clearing operations prove slower than expected: Iranian naval mines include sophisticated influence mines that are difficult to sweep, and IRGC remnants continue sporadic re-mining operations at night. Hormuz remains effectively closed through summer 2026. The economic consequences cascade: oil prices climb past $150/bbl by May, SPR reserves are drawn down to critical levels, Asian economies face fuel rationing, European industry slows dramatically, and the GCC food crisis deepens. The IEA's 'greatest energy security challenge in history' assessment proves prescient. By August, the conflict has reshaped global energy markets and trade patterns in ways that will persist for years.

title: Oil Market Adapts
description: The global energy system proves more resilient than crisis-mode forecasts predicted. Several factors converge to limit the damage: (1) Saudi Aramco activates the East-West Pipeline to full 5 Mb/d capacity, routing exports to Yanbu on the Red Sea; (2) ADNOC's Habshan-Fujairah pipeline adds 1.5 Mb/d bypassing Hormuz; (3) the US executes coordinated SPR releases totaling 60M barrels alongside IEA member drawdowns; (4) Russia and Kazakhstan quietly increase production by 1.5 Mb/d, pricing into the premium; (5) Asian demand destruction (Chinese coal/nuclear switching, Japanese LNG diversification) absorbs 2 Mb/d of the shortfall; (6) US shale producers accelerate drilling in response to $100+ prices. The net gap narrows to 2-3 Mb/d — painful but manageable. Prices stabilize at $100-110/bbl rather than spiraling to $150+. Global recession is probable but moderate rather than severe.

title: Global Recession Trigger
description: The conflict tips a global economy already under strain — elevated debt levels, persistent inflation, tight credit conditions — into synchronized recession. The oil shock acts as the classic exogenous demand-destruction trigger studied by Hamilton (1983): every major oil shock since 1973 has preceded recession. The transmission is amplified by three factors: (1) financial markets are highly leveraged with thin volatility risk premia — a 35%+ equity drawdown triggers margin calls and credit tightening; (2) central banks face an impossible trilemma — rate cuts risk inflation spiral, rate holds deepen recession, and markets are pricing in both simultaneously; (3) post-COVID supply chain fragility leaves no inventory buffer to absorb the shock. The cascading effects: emerging market currency crises (Turkey, Egypt, Pakistan first), European industrial recession, Asian manufacturing slowdown, US consumer confidence collapse. The IMF revises global growth from +2.8% to -1.5% for 2026. This is the 1973 scenario on a larger scale.
